9130:
To intermit something means to stop it for a while, with the expectation — or implication — that it will start again.

It's not a permanent stop. It's a temporary pause, a break, a suspension. The thing that intermits goes away for a time, then comes back. That idea of coming back is absolutely central to this word.

Think of it like a traffic light. It doesn't stop forever — it stops, then goes, then stops again. That pattern of stopping-and-resuming is exactly the spirit of intermit.

The verb works in two ways:

1. You intermit something (transitive — you cause the pause):

You are actively making something stop for a while.

"The doctor advised her to intermit the medication for ten days."
(= stop taking it temporarily, then resume)

"He decided to intermit his exercise routine during the cold months."
(= pause it, not quit it forever)

2. Something intermits on its own (intransitive — it pauses by itself):

The thing itself stops and starts in a natural pattern, without you doing anything to it.

"The pain intermitted for several hours before returning."
(= it went away on its own for a while, then came back)

"The rain intermitted throughout the afternoon."
(= it kept stopping and starting)
The Key Feeling of the Word

The most important thing to understand is this: intermit carries a strong sense of rhythm or pattern. When something intermits, it usually doesn't just stop once and start once. It tends to stop, start, stop, start — repeatedly. This is why the adjective form, intermittent, describes things like an intermittent signal (one that keeps flickering on and off) or intermittent pain (pain that comes and goes).

So when you use intermit, you're almost always signaling that the stopping is part of a larger pattern, not a one-time thing.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where the word sharpens up significantly.

  • Stop / cease — These don't promise that the thing will return. "The music stopped" might mean it's over forever. "The music intermitted" tells you it will come back.
  • Pause — Very close in meaning, but pause is lighter and more conversational. It often describes a single, brief break. Intermit is more formal and often implies a longer break, or a recurring cycle of breaks.
  • Suspend — Suspend usually involves a deliberate decision by someone in authority. "The court suspended proceedings." Intermit can describe both deliberate pauses and natural, self-occurring ones. Also, suspend doesn't emphasize the coming-back as strongly.
  • Interrupt — Interrupt means something from outside cuts in and breaks the flow. Someone interrupts your speech. But intermit doesn't need an external cause — the thing itself can intermit naturally.
Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

Intermit is a formal word. You will encounter it most in:

  • Medical writing — Fevers, pulses, and symptoms intermit in classic medical descriptions.
  • Legal or official documents — Proceedings, duties, or obligations may be said to intermit.
  • Classic literature and philosophy — Older writers used it freely.
  • Formal academic prose — Especially in history, science, or theology.

You would almost never hear it in casual spoken conversation. In everyday speech, people would simply say "take a break from," "pause," or "stop for a while." But when precision and formality matter — and when you want to signal that the pause is part of a pattern rather than a permanent end — intermit is the exact right word.

"The committee chose to intermit the negotiations until a new proposal was ready."

"His enthusiasm for the project intermitted whenever the workload became too heavy, but always returned."

"The ancient custom had intermitted for decades before being revived in the 1980s."

"She had to intermit her studies for a semester due to illness."

Notice in each case: the stopping is temporary, the resumption is either stated or clearly implied.

To intermit is to stop something temporarily — especially in a recurring pattern — with the clear understanding that it will begin again.

If you grasp that: the stopping is not the end, it's just a break in an ongoing rhythm — you've understood intermit completely.
9131:
Intermittent means something that keeps stopping and starting again, rather than going on without any break.

If something is intermittent, it does not happen continuously. It happens for a while, then it stops, then it comes back again, then it stops again — and this cycle repeats. The essential idea is: gaps exist. There are interruptions in between.

Think of a dripping tap. It doesn't pour out water in a steady, unbroken stream. Instead: drip... silence... drip... silence... drip. That pattern — action, pause, action, pause — is what "intermittent" captures perfectly.

The simplest way to remember this word is to think of it as a more formal, precise way of saying "on and off."

  • Intermittent pain = pain that comes and goes, rather than hurting without stopping.
  • Intermittent rain = rain that falls for a while, stops, then falls again later.
  • Intermittent Wi-Fi = a connection that keeps dropping out and reconnecting.

In every case, the thing is present sometimes and absent other times. That back-and-forth is the heart of the word.

This is an important nuance. Intermittent can refer to either:

Regular pauses — where the stopping and starting happens on a predictable schedule. A lighthouse that flashes once every 8 seconds is intermittent in a perfectly regular way.

Irregular pauses — where the stopping and starting is unpredictable. A car alarm that randomly goes off and stops throughout the night is also intermittent.

The word works for both situations. It does not tell you how often the gaps occur or how long they last. It only tells you that the thing does not happen in one continuous, unbroken stretch. The gaps exist — but their timing and length are not specified by the word itself.

Weather: "There will be intermittent showers throughout the afternoon." This means it will rain for a bit, then stop, then rain again — not a steady downpour all day.

Health and medicine: "The patient experiences intermittent chest pain." The pain is not constant. It appears, disappears, and reappears at various times. (Doctors actually find intermittent symptoms trickier to diagnose than constant ones, for exactly this reason.)

Technology: "The printer has an intermittent fault." The printer doesn't fail every single time — it works sometimes and misbehaves at other times. This kind of problem is notoriously hard to fix because it doesn't happen reliably enough to pin down.

Electricity/Power: "The village suffered intermittent power cuts during the storm." The lights weren't out permanently — they kept going off and coming back on.

Sound: "She was distracted by the intermittent beeping from the next room." Not a constant beep, but one that kept occurring at intervals.

Diet and lifestyle: You may have heard the phrase "intermittent fasting." This is a way of eating where a person alternates between periods of eating and periods of fasting (not eating) — a perfect real-world use of the word.

It helps to be clear about what this word does not mean:

It does not mean something happening constantly or continuously. A river flowing without stopping is not intermittent — it is constant or continuous. A headache that has not stopped for three days straight is not intermittent — it is persistent or sustained.

It also does not mean something that happened only once. A single power cut that lasted two hours and never happened again is not intermittent — it is simply a one-time event. Intermittent implies repetition of that stopping-and-starting pattern.

Several words are close in meaning to intermittent, but each carries a slightly different shade:

Sporadic is very similar, but it tends to emphasize that the occurrences are rare and widely spaced out — almost scattered randomly. Intermittent simply means "with gaps"; sporadic suggests the gaps are quite long and the pattern is quite unpredictable. Sporadic violence in a region means it flares up very occasionally and randomly. Intermittent violence could mean it's happening more frequently, just not non-stop.

Periodic is also close, but it tilts in the opposite direction — toward regularity. Periodic suggests the gaps follow a predictable, almost clock-like schedule. Your heart beats periodically (at a regular rhythm). Intermittent does not require that kind of regularity.

Occasional focuses more on how rarely something happens, not on the stopping-and-starting pattern. An occasional cup of coffee means you don't drink it very often. Intermittent focuses on the pattern of gaps, not on the overall frequency.

On-and-off is the informal, everyday equivalent of intermittent. They mean the same thing. "They've had an on-and-off friendship for years" = "They've had an intermittent friendship for years." Intermittent simply sounds more formal and precise.

The clearest opposites of intermittent are:

  • Continuous — going on without any break at all.
  • Constant — happening all the time, without stopping.
  • Uninterrupted — not broken by any gaps or pauses.
  • Sustained — kept up steadily over a period of time without stopping.
  • Persistent — continuing to exist without going away.

If intermittent is the flickering candle, these words describe the steady, never-wavering flame.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Intermittent = stops and starts, repeatedly, with gaps in between.

It is not constant, not one-time, and not necessarily regular or irregular — just not continuous. Whether it's rain, pain, a signal, a sound, or a problem, if it keeps coming and going rather than persisting without a break, the right word for it is intermittent.
9132:
Something happens, then stops, then happens again, then stops again — and this cycle keeps repeating. It never stays continuous.

Think of a flickering street light. It doesn't glow steadily the whole time, and it doesn't stay off the whole time. It switches — on, off, on, off. That light is behaving intermittently.

When you say something happens intermittently, you are really saying three things at once:

  1. It happens — it's present and real.
  2. It pauses — there are clear gaps where it stops.
  3. It comes back — it starts again after each pause.

This repeating cycle of happening → stopping → happening → stopping is the exact signature of "intermittently." If something only happens once and stops, that's not intermittently. If something never stops, that's also not intermittently. The word lives in the middle — the switching back and forth.

• "The Wi-Fi has been working intermittently all day."
    → The connection came on, dropped, came back, dropped again — repeatedly. It never stayed steadily connected.
  • "She cried intermittently throughout the movie."
    → She didn't cry the entire time (that would be "continuously"), and she didn't cry just once. She cried, stopped, cried again, stopped — multiple times across the movie.
  • "It rained intermittently throughout the afternoon."
    → The rain didn't pour for the whole afternoon. It rained for a while, stopped, started again, stopped again — alternating between rain and dry spells.
  • "He checked his phone intermittently during the meeting."
    → Not every single second (that would be "constantly"), and not just once. He checked it a few times with gaps in between.
  • "The old machine works intermittently."
    → It runs for a bit, stops, runs again, stops again — unreliable and unsteady.

No — and this is an important nuance.

"Intermittently" tells you the pattern (stop-start), but it does not tell you how frequent or how rare the occurrences are. Something can happen intermittently but very frequently (on for 30 seconds, off for 10 seconds, on again) — or intermittently but rarely (on for a moment, off for hours, on again briefly). Both are "intermittently."

The word is purely about the nature of the pattern (not continuous, keeps stopping and restarting) — not about how often.
Does "Intermittently" Tell You Whether the Gaps Are Equal?

No — and this is another key nuance.

The pauses between occurrences can be regular (every 10 minutes, like clockwork) or irregular (sometimes 2 minutes, sometimes 45 minutes — completely unpredictable). "Intermittently" covers both. The word only tells you there are pauses — it doesn't promise those pauses are equal.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Understanding the difference from nearby words will make your understanding razor-sharp.

Intermittently vs. Continuously / Constantly
These are direct opposites. "Continuously" means without any pause at all. "Intermittently" means with repeated stopping and restarting.

"The pump ran continuously for 8 hours." → Never stopped.
"The pump ran intermittently for 8 hours." → Kept turning on and off throughout those 8 hours.

Intermittently vs. Occasionally / Sometimes
"Occasionally" and "sometimes" just mean "not always" — they describe low frequency, but they carry no implication of a stopping-and-restarting pattern. "Intermittently" is specifically about that on-off cycling behavior.

"She occasionally reads at night." → She does it from time to time. No emphasis on starting and stopping repeatedly.

"The server crashes intermittently." → It works, crashes, recovers, crashes again, recovers — a clear back-and-forth cycle is happening.

The difference: "occasionally" is about how often; "intermittently" is about the nature of the pattern.

Intermittently vs. Sporadically
These two are the closest pair and are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: "sporadically" leans toward irregular and unpredictable timing — you can't really anticipate when it will happen next. "Intermittently" is more neutral; it can be predictable or unpredictable.

"Power cuts happen sporadically in this village." → Unpredictable — you never know when.
"Power cuts happen intermittently in this village." → The on-off pattern is clear, but the timing may or may not be predictable.

In everyday usage, most people treat these as synonyms and they'll understand you correctly either way.

Intermittently vs. Periodically
"Periodically" means at regular, somewhat scheduled intervals — there's a sense of rhythm and predictability. "Intermittently" is more neutral and doesn't require regularity.

"The doctor checks your blood pressure periodically." → At planned, regular checkup times.
"The old pipe drips intermittently." → In an uneven, unscheduled way — sometimes more, sometimes less.
The "Feel" of the Word in Real Life

When a fluent speaker hears "intermittently," they picture something unreliable or unsteady — not a total failure, but something that can't be counted on to behave consistently. There's a hint of imperfection or irregularity baked into the word.

This is why "intermittently" appears very naturally in:

  • Technology: "The app crashes intermittently." / "The signal drops intermittently."
  • Weather: "Expect intermittent showers." (Note: "intermittent" is the adjective form of the same word — "intermittently" is the adverb.)
  • Health: "The patient experiences chest pain intermittently."
  • Machines and appliances: "The heating has been working intermittently."
  • Human behavior: "She intermittently loses focus during long tasks."

In all these cases, the thing is neither fully absent nor fully present — it keeps switching.
One-Line Test to Know If "Intermittently" Is the Right Word

Ask yourself: "Is this thing switching between happening and not happening, repeatedly?"

If yes → "intermittently" fits perfectly.
If it happens just once and stops → use "briefly" or "once."
If it never stops → use "continuously" or "constantly."
If it just happens now and then without that clear stop-start cycling → use "occasionally" or "sometimes."

Intermittently means: in a way that keeps stopping and starting again, rather than going on without a break.

The thing is not constant. It is not absent. It exists in an on-off rhythm — whether that rhythm is fast or slow, regular or irregular. That is the full, precise meaning of the word.
9133:
An intern is a person — usually a student or someone who has just finished their studies — who works at a company, hospital, government office, or any other organization for a short, fixed period of time, mainly to gain real-world, hands-on experience in a field they want to work in professionally.

Think of it this way: you can read all about how surgery works in a medical textbook, but actually standing in an operating room and assisting a surgeon teaches you in a completely different way. An intern is someone doing exactly that — stepping into a real workplace to learn by doing, not just by studying.
Why Does an Intern Exist? The Core Purpose

The whole point of being an intern is learning through experience. Unlike a regular employee, who is hired primarily because the organization needs work done, an intern is there primarily to learn — even though they do real work too.

An internship fills a very important gap: the gap between the classroom and the real world. Studying teaches you theory. An internship teaches you how things actually work in practice. Employers also benefit — they get help with their work and get to evaluate talented young people they might want to hire permanently later.
What Does an Intern Actually Do?

An intern does real tasks, not fake exercises or classroom simulations. The specific work depends entirely on the field. A marketing intern at a company might help run social media accounts, research the competition, or assist with advertising campaigns. A medical intern (a newly graduated doctor) treats patients, helps in surgeries, and learns to handle clinical situations under the close supervision of experienced doctors. A journalism intern at a newspaper might write articles, conduct interviews, or help reporters with research.

In every case, the intern works under supervision — meaning a more experienced professional guides them, corrects their mistakes, answers their questions, and teaches them. An intern is not expected to already know everything. That is the whole point of being one.

They are usually new to the field. Most interns are university students (often in their second-to-last or final year), recent graduates, or people just entering a career. That said, some people switch careers later in life and take internships to get a foothold in a new field — so age is not a strict rule, but being new to the field is.

The role is temporary by nature. An internship (the period during which someone is an intern) typically lasts anywhere from a few weeks to about a year. It is not a permanent position. It has a clear start date and a clear end date. Once it ends, the intern either leaves the organization, gets offered a full-time job if they impressed the employer, or moves on to their next opportunity.

Pay is inconsistent and varies widely. Some interns are paid a regular wage; others receive only a small allowance called a stipend (just enough to cover basic expenses like transport and food); and others are completely unpaid. Whether an intern must legally be paid depends on the laws of the country and the specifics of the work arrangement. The idea of working for free is controversial, and many countries have been tightening laws around it.

The work is real and meaningful — in a good internship. In a well-run internship, the intern is given tasks that genuinely teach them something and contribute to the organization. In a poorly run one, an intern might be stuck doing trivial tasks — fetching coffee, making photocopies — that teach them nothing. This is widely criticized as a waste of an intern's time. A valuable internship puts the intern in situations where they are actually thinking, problem-solving, and practicing their craft.
Two Important Contexts Where the Word Is Used

The word "intern" appears across many fields, but there are two contexts you should know well:

In business, law, media, politics, and most other industries, an intern is a student or recent graduate doing a short work placement at a company or organization. The internship is usually part of their education or a step they take just after graduating to build their resume. For example: "She spent the summer as a marketing intern at a large advertising agency."

In medicine, particularly in countries like the United States, the word "intern" has a more specific and serious meaning. A medical intern is a doctor who has fully graduated from medical school but is in their first year of supervised practical work in a hospital. This stage is not optional — it is a mandatory part of becoming a licensed, independent doctor. A medical intern is technically qualified on paper, but they are still learning the realities of independent medical practice with oversight from senior doctors. In this context, the word carries a lot more weight and formality than it does in the business world.
How an Intern Differs from Similar Roles

Several words can seem similar to "intern" but mean something different. Understanding these differences will sharpen your understanding of the word.

Intern vs. Volunteer: A volunteer works without pay purely to help a cause or organization — for example, volunteering at a food bank or a charity. Their motivation is usually giving back, not building a career. An intern, by contrast, is specifically there to gain career experience and advance professionally. Even if an intern is unpaid, they have a career-oriented purpose that a volunteer may not.

Intern vs. Apprentice: An apprentice is learning a specific skilled trade — like plumbing, carpentry, electrical work, or hairdressing — through a longer, more formal program that ends in an official qualification or certification. Apprenticeships are usually longer, more heavily regulated, and tied to working-class or technical trades. Internships are generally shorter, less formal, and far more common in white-collar or professional settings like business, law, media, or healthcare.

Intern vs. Trainee: A trainee is usually someone who has already been hired by a company and is being trained internally for a specific role within that company. A trainee is already an employee — the company has committed to them. An intern is not a permanent employee; the organization has made no commitment to keep them, and the intern has made no commitment to stay. The relationship is more exploratory on both sides.

Intern vs. Part-time employee: A part-time employee is hired to do a job on a reduced-hours basis and is compensated for performing that job. Their primary purpose is to get the work done. An intern's primary purpose is to learn — even if they are also getting work done in the process.

The internship is the name for the overall experience, period, or program. The two words are simply different grammatical forms of the same concept:

"She is an intern at the law firm." — here, intern refers to the person.

"She is doing an internship at the law firm." — here, internship refers to the experience or program itself.

You will frequently see both words used, and now you understand that they are two sides of the same coin.

Being an intern, even when unpaid, can be genuinely valuable for several reasons. It gives you real, verifiable experience you can mention in future job applications — employers value this enormously over just having a degree. You also build a professional network, meaning you meet and form relationships with real people working in your industry who might help you get a job or open doors in the future. Beyond that, you get to experience workplace culture firsthand — how offices, hospitals, or newsrooms actually operate day to day, which no classroom can truly replicate.

For many interns, the experience also serves as a long job interview. If they perform well and leave a strong impression, the organization may offer them a permanent role. In some fields, like medicine and law, completing an internship is not even a choice — it is legally or professionally required before a person can practice independently.

An intern is a person — usually a student or a new graduate — who temporarily works at an organization specifically to gain hands-on experience in a career field. They do real work, are supervised by experienced professionals, and may or may not be paid. The experience itself is called an internship. The word is used across almost every industry, from business to medicine to journalism, and its core purpose is always the same: to bridge the gap between learning about something and actually doing it in the real world.
9134:
To intern someone means to officially confine or detain a person against their will — essentially to lock them up or restrict them to a specific place — without putting them through a normal criminal trial. A government or military authority is almost always the one doing this.

The person being interned has not necessarily been proven guilty of a crime through a court of law. Instead, the authority decides, often out of fear, suspicion, or as a wartime security measure, that this person needs to be contained.

Imagine a regular prison sentence. Normally, someone commits a crime → they are arrested → they go to court → a judge or jury finds them guilty → they go to prison. There is a full legal process.

Interning someone skips or bypasses much of that process. The authority simply says: "We consider you a threat or a risk, and so we are confining you." The person is held — often in a special facility called an internment camp — not as punishment for a proven crime, but as a precautionary or political measure.

Historically, governments have interned people in situations like these:

During wartime: If Country A is at war with Country B, the citizens of Country B who happen to be living inside Country A may be interned. They are called enemy aliens. Even if they are perfectly ordinary, harmless people, the government may intern them simply because of their nationality, out of fear they could be spies or sympathizers.

For political or security reasons: A government may intern people it considers politically dangerous — dissidents, suspected rebels, or members of groups it views as threats — without waiting for a formal trial.

During civil conflict or unrest: In times of serious internal strife, authorities sometimes intern large groups of people to suppress resistance or maintain control.

During World War II, the United States government interned tens of thousands of Japanese Americans — people of Japanese descent who were living in the U.S. — by forcing them into enclosed camps. These individuals had not been tried or convicted of any crime. They were interned purely because of their ethnicity and the government's wartime fear and suspicion. This is one of the most well-known and widely studied examples of internment in history.
The Key Things That Define "To Intern"

To make sure the meaning is crystal clear, here are the defining features of this verb:

1. It is done by an authority. Only a government, military, or similarly powerful body interns people. An ordinary person or private group cannot "intern" someone — that would simply be kidnapping.

2. No full legal trial is required. This is the sharpest difference from regular imprisonment. You can be interned based on suspicion, nationality, political beliefs, or perceived risk — not necessarily because a court found you guilty of a specific crime.

3. It is usually tied to exceptional circumstances. Internment is not everyday law enforcement. It almost always happens during wars, political crises, states of emergency, or conflicts. It is considered an extreme measure.

4. It is not permanent by design. Internment is typically meant to last for the duration of a crisis (e.g., the war), after which the interned people may be released. This is different from a life sentence, for example.

5. It can affect groups, not just individuals. Unlike a normal criminal prosecution, which targets one specific person for one specific act, internment is often applied to entire categories of people — all citizens of a certain country, all members of a certain group, etc.
The Feeling and Weight of the Word

"To intern" is a serious, heavy word. It almost always carries a negative connotation, because it represents the use of power to restrict human freedom without the full protection of law. When you read that a government "interned" a group of people, it is a signal that something harsh, controversial, or even unjust may have occurred. Historians, human rights advocates, and legal scholars often examine cases of internment critically.

Once you know the verb, these connected words will make immediate sense to you:

  • Internment (noun) — The act or condition of being interned. "The internment of civilians during the war was widely condemned." Think of it as the name for the whole situation or policy.
  • Internee (noun) — The person who has been interned. "The internees were held in camps for three years." Just as an employee is someone who is employed, an internee is someone who is interned.
  • Internment camp (noun phrase) — The physical place where interned people are held. It is a guarded facility, separate from ordinary prisons, set up specifically to hold internees.
How to Spot It in a Sentence

Here are a few example sentences showing the verb in action:

  • "The government decided to intern all foreign nationals living in the border region."
  • "Thousands of civilians were interned during the conflict and held without charge."
  • "The military had the authority to intern anyone suspected of collaboration with the enemy."

In each case, notice that a powerful body is doing the interning, the people being interned have not gone through a normal trial, and the context involves some kind of crisis or conflict.

You may already know the word intern as a noun — a student or recent graduate working at a company to gain experience. That is a completely separate word that just happens to be spelled and pronounced the same. The verb "to intern" (meaning to confine) and the noun "intern" (meaning a trainee worker) are unrelated in meaning. Always look at the context of the sentence to know which one is being used. If someone says "She was interned for two years," they almost certainly mean she was confined — not that she had a job placement.
9135:
Internalization is the process by which something that exists outside of you gradually becomes a genuine part of inside you — absorbed into your mind, your values, your habits, or your personality so completely that it no longer feels like a foreign rule or borrowed idea. It feels like your own.

Think of it like this: imagine you're handed a plant. At first it sits on your windowsill — it belongs to you, but it's still separate from your garden. Then you plant it in the soil. It takes root, spreads, and eventually becomes inseparable from the rest of your garden. That movement — from sitting outside to being rooted inside — is the essence of internalization.

This is the most common use of the word. Here, internalization describes how a person absorbs beliefs, values, or behaviors from the world around them and makes them genuinely their own.

Consider a child learning not to lie. In the beginning, the child is honest because they fear punishment — the motivation comes from outside (parents, rules, consequences). Over time, if all goes well, honesty stops being a rule the child follows and becomes a value the child holds. They don't lie not because someone is watching, but because they have genuinely come to believe that honesty matters. That shift — from obeying an external rule to owning an internal belief — is internalization.

The clearest sign that internalization has happened: you no longer need the external pressure or reminder. The belief or behavior now lives inside you and runs on its own.

Internalization is also how we absorb skills deeply, beyond the surface level.

When you first learn to drive, every action demands conscious effort: check the mirror, press the clutch, steer, check again. Your instructor is essentially an external guide — the knowledge lives outside you and you're borrowing it. With practice, these actions become automatic. You no longer think about them. The skill has been internalized — it is now a natural, effortless part of how you function.

The same applies to language. A learner consciously applies grammar rules: "Is this word plural or singular? Do I add an 's' here?" A fluent speaker doesn't think about any of this — they've internalized the patterns so completely that correct usage simply feels right, and incorrect usage feels wrong, like a false note in a familiar song.

People don't just internalize personal values — they internalize the norms and expectations of the society around them.

Think about how most people feel uncomfortable or embarrassed when they break a social norm, like speaking loudly in a quiet library or showing up much later than agreed. Nobody needs to scold you in that moment. The discomfort comes from within. That's because you have internalized the norm. It's no longer a written rule somewhere — it has become part of how you naturally understand right and wrong behavior in that context.

This is how culture gets inside people. Through family, school, religion, friendships, and media, societies pass their norms and expectations down, and individuals gradually absorb them. The result is that people largely regulate their own behavior without needing constant external enforcement — because the "rules" are no longer experienced as rules at all. They've become automatic.

In economics, internalization has a specific and important meaning. It refers to the moment when a cost or benefit that was previously external — meaning it affected others but wasn't accounted for by the person or company causing it — becomes something that person or company must now bear themselves.

The classic example is pollution. A factory dumps waste into a river. The harm this causes to health, to nature, and to communities is a real cost — but the factory doesn't pay for it. Society bears it. This unclaimed cost is called a "negative externality" — it sits outside the factory's financial world.

When a government introduces a pollution tax, something fundamental changes: the factory is now made to pay for the harm it causes. That cost has been brought inside the factory's accounting. The damage is no longer someone else's burden to absorb. This is what economists mean when they say the externality has been "internalized."

In a deeper psychological sense, internalization refers to how we absorb aspects of important people in our lives — especially parents or caregivers — into our own inner mental world.

Many people notice they carry a parent's voice in their head: words of encouragement, criticism, or caution that replay when they face certain situations. That inner voice is an internalization. The actual person may not be present, but their words, tone, and attitude have been absorbed into the person's psyche and continue to influence how they think and feel — about themselves, about the world, about what they deserve.

This is a more layered form of internalization — not just absorbing a value or a skill, but absorbing an entire relationship or emotional presence.

Understanding a word's opposite often sharpens what the word itself really means.

The opposite of internalization is externalization — the process of pushing something internal outward. Blaming others for a failure you know is yours (pushing internal guilt outward) is an externalization. Creating art to express an inner emotion is an externalization. If internalization is "taking the outside in," externalization is "pushing the inside out."

Internalization always describes the same fundamental movement: something external crossing over and becoming genuinely internal.

Whether it's a value you absorb so deeply you no longer need reminders, a skill that becomes second nature, a cultural norm that shapes your behavior without you realizing it, an economic cost that a business is made to own, or a loved one's voice that lives permanently in your mind — the mechanism is always the same.

One final distinction worth holding onto: something truly internalized is not merely memorized, performed, or obeyed on the surface. A person who follows a rule only because they'll be punished has not internalized it. A person who follows it because they genuinely believe in it has. That depth, that genuineness, that sense of it now being a real part of you rather than something imposed on you — that is what makes internalization the powerful and precise word that it is.
9136:
To internalize something means to take something that exists outside of you — a rule, a belief, a value, a feeling, a skill — and absorb it so deeply that it becomes a natural, automatic part of who you are on the inside.

Think of it as a journey something makes: it starts outside you, and through time, repetition, or deep personal experience, it travels inward and settles into your mind, your instincts, or your identity. Once internalized, it no longer needs to be pushed on you from the outside. It simply lives in you.

This is the heart of the word, so understand this well.

Imagine a child being told, "Don't hit other people." At first, the child obeys because a parent is watching, or because they fear punishment. The rule is external — it comes from outside, and it works only because of outside pressure. The moment no one is watching, the child might still hit.

But over years, something changes. The child begins to genuinely feel that hurting others is wrong. They feel bad even when no one is watching. The rule is no longer just a law imposed on them — it has become a part of their own conscience, their own values. They have internalized it.

This is the shift internalize always describes: something moves from being an external force acting on you, to an internal part of you that acts on its own.

1. Values and Beliefs
This is the most common use. When you internalize a value, you don't follow it out of obligation or fear — you follow it because you genuinely believe it.

  • A student is taught to always cite their sources. At first, they do it to avoid getting caught for plagiarism. Years later, they do it automatically because they've internalized the value of intellectual honesty. They'd feel uncomfortable not doing it.
  • Someone grows up hearing "treat others kindly." If they only follow this when someone is watching, they haven't internalized it. If they are kind even when it costs them something and nobody is watching, they have.

2. Social Norms and Cultural Messages
Societies teach people how to behave, think, and see themselves — often silently, through media, family, and community. People internalize these messages without even realizing it.

  • A woman grows up in a culture that constantly tells her she must be quiet and agreeable to be liked. Over time, she begins to genuinely believe she should not speak up, even when she has every right to. She has internalized a cultural message to the point where it feels like her own natural thought, not something that was put in her.
  • This is why internalization can be powerful in a negative sense too — people can internalize harmful ideas about themselves or others (like prejudice, self-doubt, or shame) without being aware of it.

3. Criticism and Feedback
When you internalize criticism, you don't just hear it and move on — you absorb it into your self-image. It changes how you see yourself.

  • If a teacher repeatedly tells a student, "You're not a math person," and the student internalizes this, they begin to carry that belief as part of their identity. They stop trying, not because they can't do math, but because they have accepted the label as a truth about themselves.
  • This is why "don't internalize every piece of criticism" is common advice — it means: hear it, evaluate it, but don't let it automatically become part of how you see yourself.

4. Skills and Knowledge
In learning, to internalize a skill means to practice it so thoroughly that it stops requiring conscious effort and becomes second nature.

  • A beginner driver has to think about every action: check mirror, signal, turn the wheel. After years of practice, they do all of this without thinking. The skill has been internalized — it has moved from their conscious mind into automatic behavior.
  • A musician who has internalized music theory no longer has to stop and mentally calculate chords. It flows naturally because it has become part of how they hear and think about music.

5. Lessons and Experiences
Sometimes life teaches us something through experience, and we truly take it in — not just as a fact we know, but as something that shapes how we approach the world going forward.

  • Someone goes through a difficult period and comes out of it genuinely believing that small daily habits matter. They haven't just learned this as a piece of advice — they've internalized it. It now quietly guides their decisions every day.

A useful way to know whether internalization has happened: ask yourself whether the behavior, belief, or feeling would exist even if all external pressure were removed.

  • Do you work hard only when your boss is watching? → Not internalized.
  • Do you work hard because you genuinely value doing things well? → Internalized.
  • Do you avoid lying only when you might get caught? → Not internalized.
  • Do you feel genuinely uncomfortable lying even when there's zero chance of consequences? → Internalized.

The mark of internalization is that the external source (the teacher, the parent, the rule, the reward, the threat) is no longer necessary. The value, belief, or habit has become self-sustaining inside you.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Understand — To understand something means you grasp it intellectually in your mind. You can understand a rule without internalizing it. Internalization goes deeper; it changes how you feel and act, not just what you know.
  • Memorize — Memorizing is storing information so you can recall it. You can memorize "honesty is important" without internalizing it at all. Internalization isn't about memory — it's about the idea becoming part of your character.
  • Accept — Accepting something means you agree with it or stop resisting it. Internalization often involves acceptance, but it goes further: after internalizing, the idea doesn't just sit there accepted — it acts, shaping your feelings and behavior from within.
  • Believe — Believing is close, but internalization implies an even deeper level. You can say you believe something but still act against it. When you truly internalize it, your beliefs and actions align naturally, without effort or reminder.

To internalize something is to make it yours — fully, deeply, from the inside out. It starts as something external (a rule, a belief, a lesson, a skill, a message) and becomes so much a part of you that it guides you automatically, quietly, and independently of any outside force. It is the difference between following a rule because someone is watching and following it because you believe it — because it has become part of who you are.
9137:
Internecine describes a conflict, struggle, or fight that happens within a group — meaning the people fighting each other are on the same side, or at least belong to the same larger group. It is the adjective you use when members of the same family, team, organization, nation, or community turn against each other.

Think of it this way: a war between two different countries is just a war. But a war where factions of the same country are killing each other — that is internecine. The destruction comes from within.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is the phrase "within the same group." That is what makes a conflict internecine. It is not about outsiders attacking you. It is about insiders attacking each other.

The second important quality is that internecine conflicts tend to be particularly bitter, destructive, and damaging. This is almost always implied by the word. When you call a conflict internecine, you are suggesting it is not a mild disagreement — it is a fierce, often ugly, deeply damaging struggle that tears the group apart from the inside.

The word works in two closely related ways, and both are correct:

1. Mutually destructive conflict within a group
This is the fullest sense of the word. The conflict is both internal (within a group) and mutually harmful (both sides damage each other and, in the process, weaken or destroy the group as a whole). A civil war is the classic example — the nation destroys itself by fighting within itself.

2. Simply: internal, destructive conflict
In everyday modern use, "internecine" is often used more broadly to describe any fierce internal conflict within a group, even without implying total mutual annihilation. The emphasis is on the inward direction of the fighting — members of the same body turning on each other.

Both uses are valid. The word always carries the idea of internal conflict, and almost always implies serious, damaging destruction.
Examples That Show It in Action

Here are examples across different contexts, from literal to figurative:

  • "The political party was torn apart by internecine warfare between its two main factions."

Here, two groups within the same party are fighting each other so viciously that the party itself is being destroyed. Not an outside enemy — internal fighting.

  • "The medieval kingdom collapsed not from foreign invasion, but from internecine conflict among the royal family."

Brothers, cousins, and nobles all belonging to the same ruling family were killing and betraying each other.

  • "The tech company's internecine battles between its product teams delayed the launch by two years."

This is a more figurative, everyday use. Different departments within the same company are fighting each other so destructively that real damage results. No weapons — but the spirit of the word applies perfectly.

  • "History is full of revolutionary movements destroyed by internecine struggles before they ever achieved their goals."

People fighting for the same cause end up turning on each other, and the movement collapses from within.

This is important, because the word is sometimes misused.

  • It does not simply mean "very violent" or "extremely deadly" in general. A brutal war between two separate nations is not internecine just because it is bloody.
  • It does not mean a conflict between two different, opposing groups. If two rival companies fight each other, that is not internecine — they are not part of the same group.
  • It is not a synonym for "internal disagreement" of a mild or routine kind. Internecine implies real, damaging, destructive conflict — not just a difference of opinion at a meeting.

The word loses its meaning if you strip away either the "within the same group" part or the "destructive" part.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

When a writer or speaker chooses the word "internecine," they are doing more than just describing a conflict as internal. They are passing a quiet judgment — signaling that this is a wasteful, self-defeating kind of conflict. There is often a sense of tragedy attached to it: a group that could have been strong is destroying itself from within. The word carries a weight of futility and ruin that a neutral word like "internal dispute" does not.

This is why "internecine" appears most often in writing about politics, history, war, religion, and organizations — places where internal divisions have historically caused enormous damage.

Internecine almost always appears before a noun describing a conflict:

  • Internecine war / warfare
  • Internecine conflict
  • Internecine struggle
  • Internecine feud
  • Internecine battle
  • Internecine rivalry

You would say: "The party was consumed by internecine conflict," not "The conflict was internecine between two separate parties."
Internecine means: relating to a destructive conflict that occurs within a group, where members of the same body fight and harm each other, often to the ruin of the group itself.
9138:
Internment is the act of officially confining or imprisoning a person — or more often, an entire group of people — without charging them with a specific crime and without giving them a proper trial.

It is something a government or authority does to people it considers a danger or a threat, typically during a war, a political crisis, or a national emergency. The people being held have not necessarily done anything wrong. They are confined simply because of who they are — their nationality, their ethnicity, their religion, or their political beliefs.
What Makes Internment Different from Ordinary Imprisonment

This is the most important distinction to understand.

When someone is imprisoned in the normal legal sense, there is a process: they are accused of a specific crime, they go to court, evidence is presented, and a judge or jury decides whether they are guilty. Only then are they locked up.

Internment skips all of that. There is no charge. There is no trial. There is no verdict. The authority simply decides — often by government order — that a certain group of people is a risk, and rounds them up. This is why internment is considered by many to be a deeply unjust practice, even when the government doing it argues it is "necessary" for safety or security.

It is collective, not individual. Ordinary imprisonment targets a specific person for a specific act. Internment targets people as a group, based on a shared characteristic. If you belong to that group, you can be interned — regardless of whether you personally have done anything wrong.

It is authorised by the state. Internment is not kidnapping or an illegal act carried out in secret. It is an official, government-sanctioned policy. This is what separates it from other forms of unlawful detention.

It is indefinite. Internment does not come with a fixed sentence. Interned people are typically held for as long as the authority decides it is necessary — which in practice can mean months or years.

It usually happens during emergencies. Governments most commonly justify internment by pointing to a war, a security threat, or a state of emergency. The argument is usually that the normal pace of law is too slow, and that holding these people is necessary to protect the public.

The clearest and most famous example is the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941, the United States government, fearing that Japanese Americans might be loyal to Japan, forcibly relocated around 120,000 people of Japanese descent — most of whom were American citizens — into internment camps. They lost their homes, their businesses, and their freedom, not because of anything they had done, but purely because of their ancestry. The US government later formally acknowledged this as a grave injustice.

Similarly, the British government interned hundreds of people in Northern Ireland in the 1970s during the height of the conflict known as "The Troubles." Suspected members and supporters of the IRA were held without trial. This policy was deeply controversial and is widely regarded as having worsened the conflict rather than helped it.

During both World Wars, many countries also interned civilians who were nationals of enemy countries — for example, German or Austro-Hungarian immigrants living in Britain or the United States were sometimes interned simply because of their national origin.

There is also a legally recognised and more neutral form of internment: the internment of prisoners of war (POWs). Under international law (specifically the Geneva Conventions), soldiers captured during a war can be lawfully held by the opposing side until the conflict ends. This is also called internment, though it is treated separately from civilian internment and comes with specific protections.

A person who is interned is called an internee. The facility where internees are held is called an internment camp. These camps vary enormously — from basic, fenced enclosures to more elaborate facilities — but the defining feature is always the same: people are held there against their will, without trial.
The Moral and Legal Weight of the Word

It is important to understand that internment carries a heavy negative connotation in modern usage. While governments have historically defended it as a wartime necessity, it is now widely seen as a violation of fundamental human rights — specifically the right to liberty and the right to a fair trial. Many international human rights frameworks and legal scholars consider mass civilian internment, particularly when based on ethnicity or religion, to be a form of persecution.

When you hear or read the word "internment" today, it almost always appears in a context where someone is being critical of a government's actions, examining a historical injustice, or debating the limits of state power.

To see how the word is used naturally:

  • "The internment of Japanese Americans during World War II remains one of the darkest chapters in US history."
  • "Human rights organisations condemned the government's policy of internment without trial."
  • "Survivors of the internment spoke about the years they lost, imprisoned for no crime."

In short, internment is the official, government-ordered confinement of people — usually a group — without trial or charge, most often during a war or crisis. It differs from ordinary imprisonment because it requires no proof of wrongdoing and targets people based on who they are, not what they have done. It is a word that sits at the intersection of law, politics, and human rights, and it almost always signals a serious — and often condemned — exercise of state power over individuals.
9139:
"Interpersonal" describes anything that exists or happens between two or more people — their relationship, how they interact, how they communicate, how they affect each other, and how they treat each other.

That's the whole idea.

Imagine two people standing face to face. Between them is an invisible space. That space is where greetings happen, where arguments break out, where trust builds up, where feelings get shared, where bonds form — or break. Anything that lives in that between space is what "interpersonal" refers to.

The word is always about at least two people and what happens between them. It is never about a single person alone.

The word "interpersonal" almost always pairs with another noun to describe something specific that exists between people. Here are the most important combinations:

Interpersonal skills — These are your abilities to interact well with other people. Listening carefully, speaking clearly, showing empathy, resolving disagreements calmly, making others feel comfortable — all of these are interpersonal skills. When a job posting says "strong interpersonal skills required," the employer wants someone who works well with people, not just someone who is technically good at their tasks.

Interpersonal relationships — The bonds and connections you have with specific people in your life — friends, family, colleagues, romantic partners, neighbors. These relationships form through repeated interaction and shared experience over time.

Interpersonal communication — The process of sharing information, emotions, or ideas directly with another person. A face-to-face conversation, a phone call, a heartfelt letter — these are all forms of interpersonal communication. The emphasis is that the exchange is happening person-to-person, directly.

Interpersonal conflict — When two people clash, disagree, or have tension between them. A fight between siblings, a dispute between coworkers, a misunderstanding between friends — all of these are interpersonal conflicts.

Interpersonal dynamics — The patterns of behavior, power, and influence that develop between people over time. For example, in a team at work, some people naturally lead, others follow, some clash with each other — these shifting patterns of interaction are the interpersonal dynamics of that group.

Understanding what the word does not mean is just as important as knowing what it does mean.

Personal (without the "inter-") refers to something belonging to or concerning one individual alone. Your personal opinion is yours alone. Your personal space is your own. The moment another person enters the picture and there is an exchange between you two, it becomes interpersonal.

Social is a much broader word. It refers to society as a whole, large groups, or life among people in general. "Social behavior" is how people behave in society broadly. "Interpersonal behavior" is specifically how one person behaves toward another specific person. Interpersonal is more intimate and direct; social is wider and more general.

Intrapersonal is a closely related but opposite word — it means within a single person: your inner thoughts, self-awareness, internal emotions, and self-talk. Intrapersonal is inside one person; interpersonal is between people. Think of it this way — your inner monologue is intrapersonal; the conversation you have out loud with someone else is interpersonal.

"Interpersonal" is a formal to semi-formal word. It is very common in psychology, therapy, business, HR, and academic writing. In casual everyday speech, people tend to say simpler things like "people skills," "relationship problems," or "getting along with others" instead. But when you read or hear "interpersonal," know that it's just a precise, sophisticated way of pointing to that same idea — whatever is happening between people.

• "She has excellent interpersonal skills — everyone feels heard when they talk to her."
  • "The team's interpersonal conflicts were hurting their productivity."
  • "Therapy helped him build stronger interpersonal relationships."
  • "Good interpersonal communication is the foundation of any healthy friendship."
  • "The new manager found it hard to navigate the existing team's interpersonal dynamics."
  • "Teaching children interpersonal skills early helps them handle friendships and conflicts better."
The One Rule to Remember Forever

Whenever you see the word "interpersonal," simply ask yourself: Is this about what happens between people? If yes, "interpersonal" is the right word. It always and only refers to the connection, interaction, communication, or relationship that exists between two or more people — never to one person in isolation.
